blocks.text: Coquitlam Acreages: streets and boundaries

items.t: Coquitlam's acreage ground is its northeast: the large rural parcels on upper Burke Mountain and along Coast Meridian Road and Hazel Drive, east of the Coquitlam River and below Pinecone Burke Provincial Park.

The park is the hard northern boundary: the Northwest Burke Vision records the 38,000-hectare (94,000-acre) Pinecone Burke Provincial Park to the northeast, with primary access through the vision area off Harper Road via Coast Meridian Road.

The board sub-area name for most of this ground is Burke Mountain; the planning frame is the Northeast Coquitlam Area Plan and its Partington Creek Neighbourhood Plan, which covers the eastern Burke Mountain lands between Cedar Drive and Victoria Drive.

blocks.text: Coquitlam Acreages: the housing stock

items.t: Northeast Coquitlam acreage is old large-lot stock, not a subdivision product: individual rural parcels on the Burke Mountain slopes that predate the neighbourhood plans, with no named acreage subdivision and no bare-land strata acreage community verified for this ground.

Servicing is the dividing line between parcels: the Northwest Burke Vision identifies "Water Service Constrained Lands" inside its roughly 400-hectare vision area, so two similar-sized parcels can differ completely on whether City water reaches them.

Where a Partington Creek parcel is designated in the neighbourhood plan, the planned form is ground-oriented housing, not acreage retention: the plan designates land for townhousing and envisions about 10,000 to 16,500 residents across the plan area.

blocks.text: Coquitlam Acreages: rules that affect buyers

items.t: The Partington Creek wildlife corridor is now a real constraint on Burke Mountain land: the City is securing a 50-metre-wide corridor along Partington Creek, expanding to a 100-metre buffer at a wildlife "hot spot," to protect the movement connection between Pinecone Burke Provincial Park, Minnekhada Regional Park and Burke Mountain green spaces.

The corridor land is being transferred to City ownership and designated as parkland as development proceeds, so a creek-side acreage's developable area can shrink at rezoning, not just at building permit.
Coquitlam's planning frame changed in 2026: the streamlined Interim OCP (Bylaws 5511/5512, adopted April 27, 2026) supersedes OCP No.

blocks.text: Coquitlam Acreages: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: The wildlife corridor is being bought with development, not taxes: the City states the first phase is secured through three related Burke Mountain development projects at no cost to taxpayers, using the development approval process.

The corridor followed a 15-month City-commissioned wildlife monitoring study, and the first development proposal inside it received first reading on May 25, 2026 and second and third readings after a June 22, 2026 public hearing — about 30% of the identified corridor would be protected if that project proceeds.
The three corridor projects together include more than 400 townhouse units, transportation improvements and added parkland, and the project also expands Knoll Park.
Minnekhada Regional Park, in Port Coquitlam, is the second anchor of the corridor system, east of the Burke Mountain lands across the Pitt River lowlands.

School District No. 43 (SD43) catchments are address-based up here too: Smiling Creek Elementary at 3456 Princeton Avenue serves the Burke Mountain side, but run the exact acreage address in the SD43 locator before marketing a school.

blocks.text: Coquitlam Acreages: development and new projects

items.t: Partington Creek wildlife corridor projects (Burke Mountain, between Cedar Drive and Victoria Drive): three related development projects delivering more than 400 townhouse units plus the corridor's first phase. STATUS: first proposal through second and third readings after the June 22, 2026 public hearing; City news release July 27, 2026; read 2026-11-03.

Northwest Burke Vision: the City's 30-plus-year framework for the roughly 400-hectare northwest Burke area, identifying four potential future neighbourhood planning areas and improved Pinecone Burke Provincial Park access. STATUS: vision adopted as the guiding framework; neighbourhood plans phased, read 2026-11-03.

blocks.text: Coquitlam Acreages: costs and taxes

items.t: Coquitlam's 2026 Class 1 Residential total municipal rate is $2.2756 per $1,000 of assessed value ($2.1993 municipal services plus $0.0763 drainage), and the grand total with other governments is $3.8520 per $1,000.
2026 property taxes were due July 2, 2026, with a 5% penalty after that date and a further 5% after September 15, 2026; utility bills were due March 31, 2026.
Coquitlam is a designated taxable area for the provincial Speculation and Vacancy Tax, so a vacant acreage held by a non-exempt owner is inside the declaration system.

blocks.text: Coquitlam Acreages: getting around

items.t: Coast Meridian Road and David Avenue are the through-routes for the Burke Mountain acreage ground, and Harper Road off Coast Meridian Road is the primary access to Pinecone Burke Provincial Park.

blocks.text: Coquitlam Acreages: risks and due diligence

items.t: Creek and corridor risk is mapped, not guessed: Partington Creek, Hyde Creek and Smiling Creek watercourses cross the vision area, and the City warns its watercourse information may not show every watercourse — a parcel survey and riparian check decide the real setbacks.

Servicing risk is the second map: the "Water Service Constrained Lands" in the Northwest Burke Vision tell you where City water does not yet reach, but the map does not price an extension — that figure comes from the City for the specific parcel.

faq.q: Is Coquitlam a buyers’ or sellers’ market?
faq.a: In October 2026 houses in Coquitlam had a sales ratio of 14%, which the reports’ scale reads as a balanced market, and condos and townhomes 16%, which the reports’ scale reads as a balanced market. On the reports’ scale under 12% favours buyers, 12% to 20% is balanced and over 20% favours sellers.
